title: Measurement and Hardware
intro: On a real device a quantum reservoir's features are not numbers you can read off: each one is an expectation value estimated from repeated destructive measurements, and that single fact sets the cost, the protocol and the accuracy of every physical QRC. This chapter covers the measurement problem, the protocols that work around it, the platforms that have run QRC, and how to count what a run really costs.

blocks.text: Everything before this chapter treats a quantum reservoir as a mathematical object: a channel $\mathcal T_{s}$ applied to a density matrix, and features $x_{k,i}=\operatorname{Tr}(O_i\rho_k)$ that are exact numbers. A real device offers none of that. It hands you single measurement outcomes of $+1$ or $-1$; the act of measuring changes the state that carried the memory; and the dynamics are whatever the hardware does, not what the Hamiltonian says. This chapter is about the distance between the model and the machine, and how experiments are designed to cross it.

The chapter assumes the vocabulary of Getting Started (#/qrc/start): a reservoir, a readout, ridge regression, memory capacity, and the small two-qubit reservoir of A Quantum Reservoir Worked by Hand (#/qrc/start/quantum-reservoir-by-hand). The models themselves are introduced in Quantum Reservoir Models (#/qrc/models) and the open-system tools (channels, measurement as a channel) in Open Quantum Systems Toolkit (#/qrc/open-systems). On the quantum side, the Born rule (Measurement and the Born Rule (#/quantum/foundations/measurement)) and mixed states (Mixed States (#/quantum/many-body/mixed-states)) are the two pages worth having read.

items: Features are estimated, not read. One measurement of $Z_i$ returns $\pm1$; the estimate of $x=\langle Z_i\rangle$ from $S$ shots has standard deviation $\sqrt{(1-x^2)/S}$. Shot noise is often the dominant error in QRC experiments.

Measurement destroys memory. Measuring all qubits in the computational basis replaces the state by its diagonal and erases every coherence. In the 4-qubit example of the first page the memory capacity falls from 3.84 to 1.96.

The dynamics are not the ideal Hamiltonian. Gate-based devices run a compiled, noisy circuit; analog devices drift. For a reservoir this matters less than for an algorithm, because the readout is trained on whatever the device does, but the device must do the same thing every time.

blocks.text: The first two facts interact. One run gives one bitstring per measurement and measuring wrecks the state, so the obvious way to get the feature vector at every step $k$ is to rerun the sequence up to $k$, $S$ times, for each $k$. That is $S\,T(T+1)/2$ evolution steps for a series of length $T$, which is why most early experiments used short series.
The order to read it in

items: Measurement Back-Action and Shot Noise (#/qrc/hardware/measurement-back-action): what one shot returns and what it costs, what a measurement does to the state, the restart protocol and its window, and why shot noise acts like a ridge penalty. Start here: every other page uses its formulas. About an hour.

Online Measurement Protocols (#/qrc/hardware/online-protocols): three ways of reading the reservoir while it runs (weak measurement with a Gaussian pointer, partial measurement with reset, and ensemble readout), each worked out with its Kraus operators and its price. About an hour.

Gate-Based Devices (#/qrc/hardware/gate-based-devices): how to compile a spin reservoir into CNOTs and rotations, why Trotter accuracy does not matter for a reservoir, how device noise supplies fading memory and what it costs in shots. About an hour.
Analog Platforms (#/qrc/hardware/analog-platforms): NMR ensembles, Rydberg arrays, Kerr oscillators and driven-dissipative lattices, with two small numerical experiments. About an hour.

Resource Accounting (#/qrc/hardware/resource-accounting): the wall-clock cost model, the shot budget a task needs, features per shot, the cost of classical simulation, and a pre-flight checklist. About 45 minutes.

blocks.text: Reading all five with the exercises takes roughly four to five hours. If you have one evening, read the first page fully and the cost model of the last page; those two give you the language to read any experimental QRC paper. The gate-based and analog pages are surveys with worked numbers, and can be read in either order after the protocols.

items: Shot noise: $\sigma(\hat x)=\sqrt{(1-x^2)/S}\le1/\sqrt S$. One shot is $\pm1$; the mean of $S$ is an unbiased estimate of $\langle Z\rangle$.
Non-selective measurement: $\Delta(\rho)=\sum_b|b\rangle\langle b|\rho|b\rangle\langle b|$ keeps the diagonal and erases coherences.
Restart cost: $N_{\text{runs}}=S\,T$ and $N_{\text{steps}}=S\,T(T+1)/2$, or about $S\,T\,w$ with a window $w\ge\ln(1/\epsilon)/\ln(1/\gamma)$ for contraction rate $\gamma$.
Noisy training is ridge: $\mathbb E\Vert y-(X+\eta)w\Vert^2=\Vert y-Xw\Vert^2+T\sigma^2\Vert w\Vert^2$, so the noise supplies $\lambda=T\sigma^2$.
Weak measurement of strength $\sigma$: reading variance $\sigma^2+1-\langle Z\rangle^2$, coherence multiplied by $c=e^{-1/(2\sigma^2)}$ per measurement.
Ensemble of $N$ copies: $\sigma=\sqrt{(1-x^2)/N}$, the same as $N$ shots in one run.
Trotter error of one split step: $\tfrac12[A,B]\,t^2$. Depolarising noise: features multiplied by $1-p$, shots needed grow as $(1-p)^{-2k}$ to read an input $k$ steps back.

Cost model: $t_{\text{total}}=N_{\text{runs}}t_{\text{rep}}+N_{\text{steps}}t_{\text{step}}+N_{\text{meas}}t_{\text{meas}}$; shots for noise at a fraction $\phi$ of a feature's spread $\Sigma$: $S\ge1/(\phi^2\Sigma^2)$.

blocks.text: What the chapter does not settle

The numbers in the examples come from one 4-qubit spin reservoir simulated in numpy with Gaussian approximations to shot noise, and from device times that are assumptions, not measurements of a particular machine. They show the structure of the trade-offs, which is robust, and not what a given device will do, which you must measure. The chapter also says little about error mitigation, readout error correction or calibration, which matter in practice. Whether any of this beats a classical reservoir is the subject of Quantum Advantage (#/qrc/theory/quantum-advantage); running a small case yourself is Hands-on Implementation (#/qrc/theory/hands-on-implementation).

Rule of thumb: on hardware, the useful size of a quantum reservoir is set less by its qubit count than by how many features you can estimate precisely enough within your shot budget. A feature whose variation over time is smaller than its shot noise is not worthless on its own (the readout can combine many noisy features), but it costs shots that need to be accounted for.
